draft.title: Mumbai University: how we use your personal data when you give consent
draft.summary: Mumbai University runs admissions, teaching, examinations, student services, events and alumni relations. To do this, we use some personal data about you. This notice explains each purpose we ask your consent for, what it gives you, and the data it needs. You can agree to each purpose separately. Where a student is under eighteen, we ask a parent or lawful guardian to give consent for them.

purposes.title: Admissions
purposes.uses: Lets us receive your online application, check whether you are eligible, verify your documents and contact you about your application. If the applicant is under eighteen, we ask a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent before we use the applicant's data.
dataItems: Previous academic records and mark sheets
Reservation category certificate, if you apply under a category
Parent's or guardian's name and contact details

purposes.title: Examinations and results
purposes.uses: Lets us register you for examinations, conduct them, publish your results and handle any request for revaluation of your answer papers.

purposes.title: Student records and administration
purposes.uses: Lets us keep your student record through your time at the University, including your profile, attendance, fees and documents, so that we can run your course and give you student services. If the student is under eighteen, we ask a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent before we use the student's data.

purposes.title: Online learning
purposes.uses: Gives you access to the University's online learning platform, where you can view course material, submit assignments, join discussions and see your grades.

purposes.title: Scholarships and fee concessions
purposes.uses: Lets us check whether you are eligible for a scholarship or fee concession and pay any award into your bank account.
dataItems: Parent's or guardian's details, where the scheme needs them

purposes.title: Sharing records with affiliated colleges
purposes.uses: Lets the University and your affiliated college exchange your academic and examination records so that your course, examinations and results are administered correctly.
dataItems: Student record held by your college
Submissions your college makes about you

purposes.title: Student help chatbot
purposes.uses: Lets you ask questions through the University's automated chatbot and get answers about admissions, courses and student services. The chatbot uses an automated tool to reply.
dataItems: Contact details, only if you choose to give them

purposes.title: Event and webinar registration
purposes.uses: Lets you register for University events and webinars and lets us send you joining details and updates about the event.

purposes.title: Photographs at University events
purposes.uses: Lets us take photographs and video recordings at University events in which you may appear, and use them to report on the event.

purposes.title: Alumni updates
purposes.uses: Keeps you in touch with the University after you graduate, with news, updates and invitations to alumni events.

purposes.title: Alumni donation appeals
purposes.uses: Lets us tell you about ways to support the University through donations. You can agree to updates without agreeing to donation appeals.

law.point: Every consent request must come with or after a notice telling the person the personal data and the purpose it is used for.
The notice must itemise the personal data and describe each specified purpose and what it provides or enables, in clear and plain language. Rule 3 applies from 13 May 2027.
Consent must be free, specific and informed, and limited to the data needed for the purpose; this is why each purpose, including donation appeals, is asked separately.

Some uses, such as functions under law by the State or its instrumentalities, or employment, are legitimate uses that do not need consent. They must not be presented as needing consent, so counsel must decide each record's basis.
Before processing a child's personal data (a child is anyone under eighteen, s.2(f)), the University must obtain a parent's or lawful guardian's verifiable consent.
Verifiable consent means checking that the person giving it as parent is an identifiable adult, using reliable identity and age details.

An educational institution is exempt from s.9(1) and s.9(3) only for tracking and behavioural monitoring for its educational activities or children's safety; counsel to confirm whether this affects the learning platform.
People must be able to read the notice in English or any language in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution, so translations are needed.

missingInformation: Lawful basis for all nine records is undecided; counsel must decide which rely on consent and remove any purpose that is a legitimate use under s.7, for example if the University acts as a State instrumentality.
Whether examinations, student records, affiliated college exchange and scholarships are carried out under a law or government scheme, which may make them legitimate uses rather than consent.
Whether minors can reach the examinations, online learning, chatbot, events or scholarship purposes, which would need a parent's verifiable consent.
Faculty data in the online learning and affiliated college records is likely employment-related and is left out of this student-facing notice; a person should confirm.
Whether the chatbot vendor or learning platform provider is a Data Processor under a valid contract, and what the chatbot does with chat logs.
Whether event photographs are published publicly or only used internally, so the description can be made precise.
Whether combining donation appeals with alumni updates was ever consented to under the existing alumni_updates key; counsel to confirm the split.
Translations into the Eighth Schedule languages the University will offer.

law.point: The University must let people read its notice in English or in any language in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution, which includes Marathi.
The notice must be understandable on its own, so the Marathi text must make sense without the English version beside it.
The notice must list each item of personal data and each specified purpose (the purpose named in the notice) with what it provides or enables, in clear and plain language.
Every request for consent must be in clear and plain language, with the option to read it in English or an Eighth Schedule language.
The notice must also give the link and means to withdraw consent, exercise rights and complain to the Board; TrustStack prints these, so they are not in this draft.
Rule 3 on notices applies from 13 May 2027, eighteen months after the Rules were published.
If any applicant is under eighteen, the University needs verifiable consent from a parent or lawful guardian before processing that applicant's data.

missingInformation: A fluent Marathi reader should check the translation for accuracy, tone and plain wording before publication.
The profile says 'Mumbai University' but the notice says 'University of Mumbai'; confirm the official Marathi name to use (drafted as 'मुंबई विद्यापीठ').
Confirm the preferred Marathi terms for 'alumni', 'convocation' and 'social media' match the University's existing Marathi materials.
Check that the summary's promise about withdrawing consent, rights and complaints is matched by the links TrustStack prints (Rule 3(c)).
Confirm whether any admissions applicants or event attendees may be under eighteen, and how parental consent is handled (s.9(1)) — counsel to confirm.
Confirm whether event photographs may show people other than students, applicants and alumni, which the summary does not mention.

answer.answer: This is a draft front-page narrative for Mumbai University's provisional DPDP Exposure Brief, version 1, for a person to check and edit before printing.

draft.headline: The assessment is still in progress, so much of the University's exposure is unknown rather than measured, and the remaining work has stalled.
paragraphs: This brief is provisional. It rests on the assessment in progress, 'Mumbai University DPDP Compass Baseline', and 123 questions are still unanswered. The processing register's gaps have never been generated. Most figures below therefore show what has not yet been assessed, not a settled position.

Four of the four penalty heads that apply are at stake. Their statutory ceilings total ₹700 crore. These are the maximums the Schedule to the Act allows for each breach, not a predicted fine. Only the Data Protection Board of India (the Board) can decide a penalty, and only after an inquiry. The Significant Data Fiduciary head is marked not applicable because no Government notification is recorded.

Security safeguards and the children and lawful guardians heads are not yet assessed, because no question that evidences them has been answered. Breach notification is partially mitigated: 1 personal data breach (any unauthorised use, loss or disclosure that compromises personal data) is recorded in the breach register. The 'any other provision' head is exposed because 2 processors (vendors handling personal data for the University) have no contract with DPDP clauses recorded.

There are 203 days to 13 May 2027, when most of the DPDP Rules commence. There are 3 critical and high items and 4 items in all outstanding. The University is closing about 0 actions a week, against 0.2 a week needed to finish all work by 13 May 2027. No open action is yet linked to a penalty head at stake.
bullets: Complete the 123 unanswered questions, starting with those that evidence security safeguards and children's data.
Generate the processing register's gaps so the exposure figures rest on the register, not only on unanswered questions.
Put DPDP clauses in place for the 2 processors without them, or record existing contracts; a reviewer decides whether the evidence is acceptable.
Review the 1 recorded personal data breach against the intimation duties to the Board and affected people.
Ask counsel to confirm how the children and lawful guardians duties apply to the University's students and services.
Assign owners and due dates to the 3 critical and high items and the 4 outstanding items, and link them to the penalty heads they address.
Restore a steady closing pace towards the 0.2 actions a week the brief says is needed; a person closes each action.
Note the risk that penalties in two or more instances can lead the Board to advise blocking of public access to a service.

law.point: The Board may impose a monetary penalty from the Schedule only after an inquiry finds a significant breach and the organisation has been heard.
The University, as Data Fiduciary (the body deciding why and how personal data is used), stays responsible for processing done for it by its processors.
A processor may be engaged only under a valid contract, which is why the 2 processors without DPDP clauses count against the 'any other provision' head.
After a personal data breach the Board must be told without delay, with a detailed report within the period this rule sets.
Sets extra duties for children's personal data, including verifiable parental consent and no tracking or targeted advertising directed at children.
After penalties in two or more instances, the Board may advise the Central Government to direct blocking of public access.
Most of the Rules, including notice, security, breach, retention, children and rights, commence eighteen months after publication, which is 13 May 2027.

missingInformation: The answers to the 123 open questions; until then the security and children's heads cannot be assessed.
The processing register's gaps, which have never been generated.
Owners and due dates: the brief lists no open action against any penalty head at stake.
Whether the 1 recorded breach was intimated to the Board and affected people as Rule 7 requires; the brief does not say.
Whether the 2 processors have contracts not yet recorded in TrustStack.
Counsel to confirm how s.9 and any Fourth Schedule condition for educational institutions apply to the University.
The 'upper third' indicative positions are TrustStack's exposure model, not law or a predicted fine; they are left out of the narrative.
